meta.title: Is Bitcoin About to Shock Everyone in Q4?
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · why the macro-doom case is stale · are the model labs peaking · personal agents and compute · agents need crypto rails · Q4 Wall Street FOMO · the 46-name index and agentic investing

snapshot: Jordi Visser calls the macro-doom crowd *stupid*: rates have only normalized, nominal GDP runs about **6.5%**, and Micron plus Nvidia now out-earn Ford, GM and the homebuilders combined.
Tech and tech-like names are **56%** of the S&P 500 and the AI trade shows, in his words, no rate sensitivity — the 52-week lows are in rate-sensitive staples, utilities and real estate.

Pompliano pushes back that the model labs may be peaking (falling token use per customer, falling token prices); Jordi agrees growth has passed its fastest point but expects agent-driven token demand to outrun compute next year.
Jordi's core thesis: AI agents need crypto rails — T+2 settlement is a window for agent swarms to steal money, so instant cryptographic settlement becomes a necessity.
He sees Wall Street FOMO building: three asset-manager calls this week, Goldman, Morgan Stanley and Citi racing on tokenization and stablecoins, and Q4 allocator decisions for next year.
His equal-weight 46-name crypto index is up about **50%** year to date against Bitcoin down **3.2%**; he plans an agent-driven dashboard to trade it in one click, not an ETF.
Pompliano agrees agentic, tokenized investing is the direction but expects regulation to slow it, and predicts AI firms doing crypto (and the reverse) through 2027.
Both hosts run their own businesses in this space (Jordi's subscriber service and index, Pompliano's Sylvia) — flagged in the relevant themes.

themes.status: JORDI'S CASE — THIS ISN'T THE PRE-2007 ECONOMY
themes.title: Doom-on-rates ignores that AI names now dominate the index and don't care about rates
themes.lead: Jordi argues the economy changed after the iPhone and the financial crisis, so 50-year analogies about oil and rates no longer apply.
bullets: Rates normalized rather than spiked: nominal GDP is about **6.5%**, and 10-year yields have traditionally sat about 200 basis points above it until 1997 — so today's yields are cheap against growth.

In 2015, Ford, GM and the homebuilders had almost **20x** the annual revenue of Micron and Nvidia; today Micron and Nvidia alone exceed them combined, and Nvidia's expected next-year revenue growth is almost the entire size of those groups' revenue.

Tech plus Netflix, Google, Meta, Amazon and Tesla is **56%** of the S&P 500, versus about 13% when the iPhone launched at the end of a 7-year tech bear market — so poor market breadth is a mechanical result, not a warning.
Micron's margins hit 87% in earnings this week; Anthropic and OpenAI sell compute at prices buyers accept because they need it, so he sees no rate sensitivity in the AI trade.
Staples, utilities and real estate are making 52-week lows because they trade like synthetic bonds as yields rise; Jordi and Pomp agree rate-sensitive businesses stay under pressure.
Homebuilders and carmakers are 'zombie companies' that will struggle long-term as demographics and mobility change; Buffett-style quality cash-flow value investing may have a hard time.
Pomp's counterpoint: Fed rate-hike signals marked the top in November 2021 and 2000, which is what doomers lean on — though rates and markets are both rising now.

quote.text: If you actually used AI and you saw the productivity gains, you'd recognize that the economy's changed.

themes.status: HOSTS PARTLY DISAGREE, THEN AGREE ON NUANCE
themes.title: Are OpenAI and Anthropic peaking? Falling tokens-per-customer versus a still-huge revenue base
themes.lead: Pompliano sees pressure on the model labs from falling token use and prices; Jordi says growth has peaked in rate but the labs are still the fastest-growing companies ever.
bullets: Pomp's three signals: token use per customer is turning over (Ramp AI Index spending down, OpenRouter-type metrics lower), prices are falling (Grok's newest model chart), and tokens times price equals lab revenue, which shows plateauing growth; he raised these with Dan Ives this week.

Jordi: early-2026 *token maxing* was inefficient, token costs are deflationary, and the agentic wave will explode volume — he does not call himself a lab bull and says growth has already passed its fastest point.

He cites Anthropic at an annualized run rate of $100 billion-plus, and says OpenAI plus Anthropic revenue by year-end will exceed the entire software industry's; Anthropic went from $50 billion to a multi-trillion valuation in a year and a half.
Jordi: they will not reach $1 trillion revenue, but frontier intelligence demand from biotech, nanotechnology and physical science is underestimated; Jane Street and Millennium already use Anthropic.

Pomp: Sylvia, with fewer than 10 engineers, built models more accurate than trillion-dollar labs for personal finance; customers adopt labs as an *on-ramp*, then optimize in-house, so labs must keep recruiting new customers.

Both agree on Jevons paradox (cheaper intelligence drives more use), that the easy money in AI is over, and that the labs won't capture all the value; Jordi finds Gemini error-prone and Muse good enough for basics.
Jordi stopped using his Open Claw and Hermes setups after finding Claude and OpenAI did the work better.

quote.text: You can't fade what's gone on.

themes.title: Personal agents and agent swarms will push token demand past available compute
themes.lead: Jordi expects usage to skyrocket next year while the big labs control the new compute.
bullets: Pomp: Instinct's founder (on *Invest Like the Best*) spends about 40% of his time hunting compute, is growing roughly 10% a day, and runs over $1 billion in transactions, about 40% travel.

Pomp lists the week's agent launches: Robinhood agentic trading, a new OpenAI agent product, an agent in Ryan Serhant's Simple app, Muse targeting small business, and Sylvia now taking texted commands.
Jordi's stack: Grokbot is his chief of staff, with two middle-management chiefs of staff beneath it; he says Muse changed how much he does daily.
Compute: Vera Rubin brings another efficiency step that the large labs own; per SemiAnalysis and the All-In podcast, OpenAI and Anthropic combined will own up to **50%** of compute coming online.
Jordi says Meta didn't win anything with Muse — there will be many personal AIs, and Apple's launch brings more; he guesses Apple will be better than Meta on security.

themes.status: JORDI'S THESIS — AGENTS ARE THE ECONOMIC ACTORS
themes.title: Agent swarms need instant settlement, so crypto rails beat Visa and Mastercard
themes.lead: Jordi argues slow card and wire settlement is a security hole for agents, and instant cryptographic settlement closes it.
bullets: A Friday 3pm wire settles Monday, and a card payment passes many hops; every extra second is a window for an agent swarm to intercept funds — instant settlement is the defense.
He rejects the view that Visa and Mastercard win from agents: *they have no chance* given the number of steps between buying and settling.

We didn't need altcoins or most tokens — we needed the layer ones to pull in capital and build infrastructure; with Bitcoin and Ethereum as digital collateral, Michael Saylor's capital-structure change becomes possible.
Analogy: Uber couldn't exist until the app store did; agents plus crypto will spawn innovation after innovation the same way.

Illia Polosukhin of Near (a co-author of the transformer paper) said in a 2023 *No Priors* interview that agents would be the economic actors of the future — Jordi's vision source; he also cites William Mougayar (book due in 3-6 months) and a former BlackRock executive.
Jordi has bought more crypto every day since putting Muse on his phone, and says three hedge fund and asset-manager calls this week asked about crypto.

quote.text: We didn't need the tokens. We didn't need the altcoins. We needed the layer ones to draw capital in to build out the infrastructure.

themes.title: Q4 allocator decisions, tokenization and softer rates could ignite Wall Street crypto FOMO
themes.lead: Both hosts see new buyers arriving and large allocators deciding next year's positions now, with limited vehicles to buy.
bullets: Jordi: Bitcoin above $82,000 confirmed the bull trend; asset managers who once barred the door are now *looking through it*, and FOMO starts very soon.

Allocators set next-calendar-year positions in Q4, especially the last two months, before performance pay crystallizes; but vehicles are limited to ETFs, DATs and about five public stocks — so L1s get a persistent underlying bid.
Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Citi are racing on tokenization and stablecoins; altcoin beta will come from institutions only once tokenization arrives.

Macro tailwinds: lower core PCE, a jobs report with unemployment below expectations and softer hourly earnings, a Treasury buyback and curve twist, and David Zervos reportedly brought in to help lower long-term rates; rates only need to stop rising.
Earnings season starts in two weeks and post-midterm, people may ask *why were we waiting*; Pomp riffs that crypto loves the fourth quarter.

Pomp: his tweeted call that AI profits would rotate back into Bitcoin appears to be starting, and Sylvia may be the only public company marrying AI and Bitcoin; Coinbase suits a 70/30 crypto/AI mix, Robinhood a 70/30 equities/AI mix.
Pomp's 2027 prediction: public companies start doing crypto and crypto firms do more AI.

themes.status: JORDI PLANS A ONE-CLICK AGENT PORTFOLIO
themes.title: The 46-name crypto index and the push-button agent portfolio, with regulation as the brake
themes.lead: Jordi wants subscribers to buy an equal-weight crypto ecosystem basket through an agent dashboard, while Pompliano warns the rules aren't ready.
bullets: The Visser Labs 46-name index (L1s plus many L2s, equal weight, 42 tokens and 4 public stocks) is up about **50%** year to date against Bitcoin down **3.2%** — the reverse of Bitcoin's peak, when altcoins lagged.
Jordi will build a dashboard with API keys that lets an agent buy all 46 names at once; he isn't launching an ETF and asked asset managers to partner, since the pieces span tokens and stocks.

Pomp: similar products already appear — agentic trading at eToro, Robinhood and Coinbase, Public's describe-it index builder, and Autopilot, in which he invests — but rules are written for ETFs and mutual funds, and agents may be unregulated; he expects slower progress than claimed.
Open questions: how users sell or rotate, whether platforms need legal changes, and how a decentralized ETF interfaces with regulators.

Jordi's forecast: a year from now wealth advisors face a hard spot as clients hear friends made 30x in tokens; stocks will be tokenized; he calls this a *Micron moment* where people underestimate speed.
He had expected Micron to double or perhaps triple and says the result vastly beat that (captions show '14 times'); he wants viewers researching now and will post seven podcasts this weekend.
themes.watch: Jordi markets the index to his subscribers and is seeking partners to productize it; Pompliano is an investor in Autopilot and runs Sylvia. Regulators have no stated answer yet.

takeaways.title: Test any macro-doom argument by asking whether it holds when tech is 56% of the S&P 500.
Track token volume, token price and compute supply together before judging lab revenue.
Watch Q4 allocator flows, since decisions made now set positions for next year.
Weigh settlement speed as an agent-security question, not just a cost question.
Expect rules to lag agentic and tokenized investing, and size the opportunity accordingly.

hot_takes.take: I actually think it's stupid. Podcast over.
There is absolutely no sensitivity for rates in the AI trade. None.
hot_takes.why: Absolute claim against the rates-top narrative.

hot_takes.take: I keep hearing people tell me, Visa and Mastercard are going to be the winners in this. No, they're not. They have no chance.
hot_takes.why: Calls the payment incumbents losers in agent commerce.

hot_takes.take: Home builders are going to have a tough time forever.
Do I think they're going to get to a trillion dollars in revenue? Absolutely not.
